architecture_decisions.recommendation: Extended organisation session data to include team email addresses by modifying the getOrganisationSession tRPC procedure to fetch teamEmail with email field
architecture_decisions.rationale: Team email addresses needed to be accessible on the client side for recipient matching. The organisation session is the primary source of team-related data for the current user, making it the logical place to include team email information. This ensures the data flows through the existing tRPC infrastructure consistently.
alternatives_considered: Creating a separate API endpoint for team email lookup
Fetching team email data directly from Prisma in each component
Storing team emails in local storage or cookies

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created a reusable utility function findRecipientByEmail that handles both personal and team email matching, then refactored all recipient lookup logic to use this function
architecture_decisions.rationale: Centralizing the recipient matching logic prevents code duplication and ensures consistent behavior across all components. The function accepts both userEmail and teamEmail parameters, allowing flexible matching without requiring callers to understand the business logic. This follows the DRY principle and makes future changes easier.
alternatives_considered: Creating a React hook for recipient matching
Extending the Recipient model with helper methods

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated all documents table components to use the new findRecipientByEmail utility and pass team email data through component props where needed
architecture_decisions.rationale: The documents table has multiple related components (action button, dropdown, title, main table) that all need consistent recipient matching. By updating each component to use the centralized utility, we ensure uniform behavior. The teamEmail is passed down through props in the main table to child components, maintaining the React data flow pattern.
alternatives_considered: Using React context for team email
Creating a wrapper component that injects recipient matching logic
Using a custom hook in each component

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated TypeScript types to include the new teamEmail field in organisation session response and component props
architecture_decisions.rationale: Maintaining type safety is crucial in a TypeScript codebase. The types were updated in the tRPC response schema and component props to ensure compile-time checking of the new teamEmail field. This prevents runtime errors and provides better developer experience with IDE autocompletion.
alternatives_considered: Creating loose interfaces that allow any additional properties
Not updating types and relying on runtime checks

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated the embed authoring layout mock data to include teamEmail field for consistency
architecture_decisions.rationale: The embed authoring layout uses mock data for development/testing purposes. Adding the teamEmail field ensures that the mock data structure matches the real data structure, preventing issues during development and testing. This maintains consistency across the application.
alternatives_considered: Using conditional logic to handle missing fields

implementation_summary:
The implementation addresses the team email recipient support issue through a systematic, layered approach. First, the data layer was extended by modifying the getOrganisationSession tRPC procedure to include team email addresses in the organisation session data. This ensures team emails are available on the client side through the existing data flow patterns.

Second, a centralized utility function findRecipientByEmail was created in the shared packages directory. This function encapsulates the business logic of checking both user email and team email when matching recipients, replacing the previous inline logic that only checked user email. This follows the DRY principle and ensures consistent behavior across the application.

Third, all documents table components were updated to use this new utility function. The changes were applied to the action button, dropdown, title component, and main table - ensuring that action buttons and title links properly appear for users receiving documents through team emails. The team email is passed through component props where needed, maintaining React's unidirectional data flow.

Finally, TypeScript types were updated to maintain type safety, and mock data was adjusted for consistency. The implementation leverages the existing monorepo structure, with shared utilities in packages/ and component updates in apps/remix/. This approach minimizes code duplication, maintains consistency with existing patterns, and ensures the feature works seamlessly across all parts of the documents table interface.
